steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the [bridgeLength] variable to a user input (ask for number) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How many characters will the user be able to enter?

❓ How do you think user input will be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that user input can make a project feel more engaging and exciting. Prompt them to think about other ways user input might be used in a project.
steps.instructions:
Open the tilemap and explore the design. Notice the 30 white outline tiles that will be filled in by the user so the Player sprite can cross over to the treasure.


Begin the project by asking for user input to place a certain number of tiles on the tilemap! Make a new variable named bridgeLength. Drag the [set [bridgeLength] to] block inside the [on button pressed] container.


Open Game and drag an (ask for number) value block into the [set [bridgeLength] to] block. In the parameter, type the string: “How many sections do you want to build?” 


Click + and set the max length to 1 character long.


Click ▶  and press A to see the program ask for a number.

steps.hints: ❓Did you select less than or equal to (≤) in the comparison block in the [if then] conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the project check whether the user inputted number is less than or equal to the number of open spaces left?

❓ What do you think will happen if the user inputted number is less than the array of white outline tiles? What if it’s greater than the array of white outline tiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja how the project knows how many white outline tiles remain on the tilemap. By calculating the array of all white outline tile locations, the project is able to count how many tiles are left in the bridge gap on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to check that the user input is less than the amount of open spaces left!


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on button pressed] container, under the variable block. Replace the <true> value with a <0<0> comparison block. Click the dropdown and select less than or equal to (≤). 


Drag a (bridgeLength) variable into the left parameter of the comparison block. Drag a (length of array) block into the right parameter, and replace the (list) with (array of all tile locations). Select the white outline tile. 


Now, the code will check whether the user input number is less than or equal to the amount of white outline tiles left in the project!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace (location) with a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block in the ((location) column) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What value is stored in the [startingColumn] variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [startingColumn] variable stores the playerSprite’s column location on the tilemap. This will be used to place tiles in the next steps.
steps.instructions:
Use the Player sprite’s location to set bridge tiles.


Create another variable named startingColumn. Drag a [set [startingColumn] to] block inside the [if then] conditional.


Open Scene and drag a ((location) column) block into the [set [startingColumn] to] block. Open Scene again and replace (location) with a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block. Select the Player sprite's name.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a (0-0) operator in the parameter of the [for index] loop to subtract 1 from the user input?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓At what number does a [for index] loop begin counting at?

❓Why is the ((bridgeLength) - 1) operator necessary in the [for index] loop, in order to place the correct number of bridge tiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that the [for index] loop will begin counting at 0, instead of 1. In this example, the operator is necessary because if a user inputs a value of 5, then the [for index] loop will run an additional time (6), since it begins counting at 0. Consequently, it is necessary to subtract 1 from the bridgeLength to match the user inputted number.
steps.instructions:
Use a loop to set up the bridge building code!


Drag a [for index] loop into the [if then] conditional, under the variable block. Drag a (0-0) operator into the parameter of the [for index] loop. Place a (bridgeLength) variable in the left parameter of the (0-0) operator, and type “1” in the right parameter. Because programs start counting at 0, subtracting 1 will provide the correct amount of bridge sections to build.


Add a [change [startingColumn] by] block inside the [for index] loop and leave the parameter set to 1.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the (0+0) operator to add 1 to both ((tilemap location of (sprite)) row) blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to include a (0+1) operator in the [set tile at location] and [set wall at] blocks?

❓ How many tiles are placed when the A button is pressed and the user inputs a number? Where are they placed on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can generate a variable bubble by right clicking on the [set variable to] block and selecting “create (variable)”.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can duplicate the ((location) column) block to add to the operator in the [set tile at location] and [set wall at] blocks.

💡 Because the bridge tiles should appear below the Player sprite (not on the same row), the (0+1) operator is necessary to use in the row parameter.
steps.instructions:
Use tiles to build the bridge in sections!


Drag a [set tile at location] block under [change [startingColumn] by] inside the [if then] conditional. Select the bridge tile, then drag a (startingColumn) bubble in the col parameter.


Drag a (0+0) operator into the row parameter, then place a ((location) column) block in the left parameter. Select [row], then place a (tilemap location of (sprite)) block set to the Player sprite as the (location). Type “1” in the right parameter. This will place a bridge tile to the right of the sprite’s location.


Drag a [set wall at] block into the bottom of the [for index] loop. Toggle the wall <ON>, then duplicate the (startingColumn) variable and drag it into the col parameter. Duplicate the (0+0) operator from the [set tile at location] block and place the entire block in the row parameter. 


Click ▶ and press A to build a bridge in sections when asked!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a [show long text] block to add a message to warn users about using too many bridge tiles?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ When will the project tell the user that there are too many bridge tile sections?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the logic of the [if then] conditional. If the user input is less than or equal to the number of white outline tiles on the tilemap, it will add that number of sections to the bridge. If the user input is greater than the number of white outline tiles left on the tilemap, then the project will say “too many sections!”
steps.instructions:
Add code to warn the user about using too many bridge tiles!


Click + to add an [else] condition. Drag a [show long text] block into the [else] opening. Type a string that tells the user when their number is greater than the number of tiles left, such as “Too many sections! Try a smaller number!”


Click ▶ to see what happens when too many bridge tile sections are requested.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add [game over] blocks to the two [on sprite overlaps tile] containers?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓When will the game end in a win? When will the game end in a loss?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The game will end in a win if the Player sprite reaches the treasure chest at the end of the bridge, meaning they input the correct number of bridge tiles. The game will end in a loss if the Player sprite falls into the “water”, meaning they did not input the correct number of bridge tiles.
steps.instructions:
Code win and lose conditions to the project!


Drag a [game over] block set to <LOSE> into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container set to the light blue tile. Add a [play sound] block to customize the effect!


Drag a [game over] block set to <WIN> into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container set to the treasure chest tile. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite “falls” into the water or finally reaches the treasure chest!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help your users understand how this project works?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓Why might you use a wooden sign tile to share directions with the user?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to reflect on game design, and why it might be interesting to set the directions to show when the Player sprite has overlapped a wooden sign tile, rather than immediately showing up on the screen when the project begins.
steps.instructions:
Code directions to your project!


In the [on sprite overlaps tile] container set to the wooden sign tile, add a [show long text] block with directions in a string, such as “Press A to build the bridge across!”


Drag a [set tile at location] block into the container, drag a (location) bubble into the parameter, and leave it set to the blank default tile so that the wooden sign tile disappears after the message is shown!


Click ▶ to see a message appear when the Player sprite overlaps with the wooden sign tile.
